title: Made in Europe relies on maintaining production links with the UK
gist: Oxford Economics warns the EU's proposed Made in Europe / Industrial Accelerator Act, which sets origin and low-carbon requirements for sectors like automotive and clean technology, risks disrupting deep post-Brexit UK-EU production links — quantifying UK automotive exports to the EU at €20 billion in 2024, supporting €5.6 billion in EU supplier spending, ~58,000 jobs, and €1.6 billion in tax revenue.

themes.theme: UK-EU production links persist despite Brexit

insights.claim: Parts, machinery, and services produced in the EU enter UK production facilities whose output then returns to EU customers, and Brexit changed the trading framework but did not remove these underlying production links.
insights.speaker: Stephen Foreman
insights.so_what: This establishes that UK-EU manufacturing interdependence remains structurally intact post-Brexit, meaning EU policy that reduces UK production demand has a direct, quantifiable feedback effect on EU suppliers, not just a UK-side cost.
insights.quote: Brexit changed the trading framework, but it did not remove these production links. A decision that reduces demand for UK production risks also reducing orders for its EU suppliers.

themes.theme: Scale of the automotive sector's cross-border links

insights.claim: In 2024, around €20 billion of UK automotive production was exported to the EU, associated with an estimated €5.6 billion of spending on EU-produced goods and services, supporting approximately 58,000 jobs and €1.6 billion in tax revenues, with links extending into wholesale/retail, transport, professional services, real estate, and utilities.
insights.speaker: Stephen Foreman
insights.so_what: This gives a concrete magnitude — 58,000 EU jobs and €1.6B in EU tax revenue — tied to UK automotive export demand, a quantifiable exposure for EU policymakers and investors to weigh against any Made in Europe restriction that reduces UK-sourced automotive output.
insights.quote: around €20 billion of UK automotive production was exported to the EU. That output was associated with an estimated €5.6 billion of spending on EU-produced goods and services, supporting an approximately 58,000 jobs and €1.6 billion in tax revenues

insights.claim: The cited figures are estimates of existing economic activity potentially exposed to policy change, not a forecast of actual losses, derived by tracing purchases through EU supply chains and worker wage spending using Oxford Economics' Business Economic Impact Calculator.
insights.speaker: Stephen Foreman
insights.so_what: This methodological caveat matters for interpreting the headline figures correctly: the 58,000-jobs/€1.6B numbers represent exposure, not a predicted outcome, so they shouldn't be read as a guaranteed loss forecast if the Industrial Accelerator Act proceeds.

themes.theme: The Industrial Accelerator Act's origin rules as the policy risk

insights.claim: The European Commission's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act would use public purchasing and support to favor cleaner, more resilient production, with different low-carbon or origin requirements for steel, cement, aluminium, clean technologies (batteries, solar, wind, heat pumps), and electric vehicles and their components.
insights.speaker: Stephen Foreman
insights.so_what: The sector-specific and varying nature of the proposed origin rules means the policy's impact on UK-linked production will differ materially by sector, so companies in steel, EVs, and clean-tech supply chains need sector-specific rather than blanket assessments of their exposure.
insights.quote: The European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act would use public purchasing and support to encourage cleaner, more resilient production. It proposes different low-carbon or origin requirements for steel, cement, and aluminium

insights.claim: Under the Commission's March draft, most UK content would generally count as equivalent to EU origin, but stricter conditions have been identified specifically for electric and hybrid vehicles, and the legislation remains under negotiation.
insights.speaker: Stephen Foreman
insights.so_what: EV and hybrid vehicle supply chains face a materially different (stricter) origin-rule risk than most other UK-linked sectors under the current draft, making automotive EV suppliers the segment most exposed to unfavorable rule changes as negotiations continue.
insights.quote: Under the Commission’s March draft, most UK content would generally count as equivalent to EU origin. The European Commission has identified stricter conditions for electric and hybrid vehicles, however, and the legislation remains under negotiation.
